extracted.intended_audience: startup founders and early-stage startup PR teams (YC founders)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical public-relations tactics for startup founders and teams, emphasizing founder-led storytelling, timing of announcements, pitch structure, and journalist targeting. Based on Y Combinator guidance for when and how startups should do PR.

rubrics_metrics.name: PR is about your customers and market
rubrics_metrics.description: PR is not about you — it's about your customers and your market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame stories around customer problems and market context rather than self-promotional messaging; make the audience see impact on the market or users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell stories about problems, not products
rubrics_metrics.description: Best startup stories come from talking about a problem, not a product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead with the pain point or hidden issue you discovered; then explain your solution as the natural response — avoids sounding like an ad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Founders should be the spokespeople
rubrics_metrics.description: Founders are the best spokespeople, not PR firms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use founders as primary interviewees and quote sources; authenticity from a founder voice is valued over polished agency messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build media relationships before you need them
rubrics_metrics.description: Build relationships before you need them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Network with reporters and outlets in advance so outreach feels familiar and is more likely to get pickup when you have real news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do PR for Series A+ funding announcements
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Save major funding PR for meaningful rounds (typically Series A and later) when it signals scale/momentum worth covering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do PR for genuinely new product launches
rubrics_metrics.description: Product launches with genuine new capability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only pitch product launches when there is an actual, newsworthy capability or milestone — not incremental or minor updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do PR for industry data reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Industry data report from your unique vantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have proprietary, interesting data or an industry report that reveals a newsworthy trend, that can be a launchable story angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do PR for major customer wins (with permission)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Announce large customer contracts or notable adopters only when the customer agrees and the win meaningfully validates your product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do PR for honest pivot stories
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narratives about pivots that candidly explain what was learned can be compelling — emphasize authenticity and lessons rather than spin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do PR for acquisitions or major hires
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquisitions or senior-executive hires can warrant coverage when they indicate strategic shifts or growth milestones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't do PR when pre-product
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pitching before you have a product; early-stage concept announcements rarely produce useful coverage and can set poor expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't do PR when pre-revenue without differentiation
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have no revenue and no clear differentiation, media attention is unlikely to be valuable; wait until you have demonstrable traction or uniqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't pitch minor product updates
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Save PR for substantive changes; small release notes or tiny tweaks are not newsworthy and can dilute your credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't do generic thought leadership pieces
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pitching bland, generic op-eds framed as thought leadership — reporters want news, data, or tightly scoped stories, not abstract positioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't inappropriately ride others' news cycles
rubrics_metrics.description: Trying to ride someone else's news cycle inappropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not force connections to unrelated news solely to get coverage; contrived tie-ins are often ignored or rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Founder writes the first draft of the pitch
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The founder should draft the initial pitch/email so the voice and facts are accurate; PR firms should refine, not originate, founder voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: PR firms should polish, not ghostwrite
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies can edit and improve clarity, but the quoted voice and core messaging should originate from the founder to preserve authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotes must sound like the founder actually talks
rubrics_metrics.description: Quote sounds like founder actually talks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write quotes in a conversational, believable tone that reflects the founder's real language — avoid overly corporate-sounding or invented phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Founder should be directly available for interviews
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make founders accessible to reporters; direct availability increases trust and the likelihood of richer coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Founder's public profiles must match PR claims
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the founder's LinkedIn and other public profiles support the claims in the pitch (role, experience, company association) to avoid credibility issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch subject line: ~8 words, news + entity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep subject short (~8 words) and clearly state the news plus the company/entity to signal relevance quickly in an inbox.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch paragraph 1 — state the news in one sentence
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with one clear sentence that summarizes the news; reporters should immediately understand what's new or notable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch paragraph 2 — explain "why now" concisely
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quickly justify timing or urgency: why this matters now, data points or market shifts that make it timely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch paragraph 3 — offer value (interview/demo/exclusive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Para 3: What you can offer (interview, demo, exclusive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly state what you can provide the reporter — an interview, demo, data, or an exclusivity offer — to make coverage easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include direct contact details and calendar link
rubrics_metrics.description: Sign off: phone number, calendar link.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always include a phone number and, when appropriate, a calendar link to streamline scheduling; this reduces friction for reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use origin-story angle: "Why we built X"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narratives about founding insight and the problem that motivated the product are compelling human-interest angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use humility/pivot angle: "We were wrong about X"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admitting earlier mistakes and explaining learning can produce credible, interesting stories that differentiate you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use problem-reveal angle: hidden industry problem
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose overlooked pain points or structural problems in an industry to create a newsworthy narrative and demonstrate domain expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use growth trajectory angle: from 0 to X users
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete growth narratives with data and tactics (how you scaled) attract attention — include metrics and actionable specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use unexpected-customer angle
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our biggest customer wasn't who we expected".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories about surprising customer segments or unexpected use cases can reveal broader market opportunity and humanize the company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch reporters in recommended order (hierarchy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitching Hierarchy (YC Recommended): 1. Reporter who has covered your space recently; 2. Reporter at the right outlet for your audience; 3. Trade publication covering your industry; 4. Newsletter writers in your space; 5. Wire service (only after personal pitches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize reporters who already cover your area and outlets that reach your audience; use trade press and newsletters next; only use wire services after personal outreach has been attempted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch must be specific to the journalist's beat
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor pitches to the reporter's recent coverage and beat — relevance increases pickup; avoid one-size-fits-all messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Send personal emails, not blasts
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mass, impersonal distribution; write individualized emails that show you've read the reporter's work and explain why the story fits them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer real story framing over promotional language
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame announcements as stories (conflict, learning, data) rather than marketing/press-release hype; journalists respond to narrative and news, not ads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be honest and avoid hype
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use candid, realistic claims; overstatement damages credibility and reduces long-term media relationships.
